Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 87, verses 1–5:

Meccan, and its verses are 19 [revealed after Surat al-Takwir]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

"Glorify" the name of Him, exalted and mighty: this means declaring Him transcendent above whatever meanings are not fitting for Him, which would be a deviation (ilhad) concerning His names, such as compulsion (jabr) and anthropomorphism (tashbih) and the like. For example, one should not interpret "the Most High" (al-A'la) as meaning elevation in the sense of place and literal settling upon the Throne, but rather in the sense of elevation that is dominance and power. And His name should be guarded from being made common or mentioned carelessly, rather than being mentioned with humility and veneration.

It is also permissible for al-A'la to be an attribute of "Lord" (Rabb), and of "name" (ism). Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: "Subhana Rabbiya al-A'la" (Glory be to my Lord, the Most High).

It is related in a hadith: When the verse "So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty" (fasabbih bi-ismi rabbika al-azim) was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Place it in your bowing (ruku')." Then when "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" (sabbih ism rabbika al-a'la) was revealed, he said: "Place it in your prostration (sujud)." [Narrated by Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and Ahmad, from the narration of Iyas ibn Amir from Uqbah ibn Amir.] They used to say in bowing: "O Allah, to You I have bowed," and in prostration:

"O Allah, to You I have prostrated."

"Who created and proportioned" (khalaqa fasawwa): that is, He created every thing and proportioned its creation in due measure, not bringing it forth disordered or ill-fitting, but with precision and coherence, and as an indication that it proceeds from a knowing One, and that it is the handiwork of a Wise One.

"Who determined and guided" (qaddara fahada): He determined for every living creature what suits it, then guided it to it and made it aware of the way to benefit from it. It is related that when a viper (af'a) reaches the age of a thousand years, it goes blind, and Allah had inspired it that rubbing the eye with the tender leaves of fennel (al-raziyanaj) restores its sight. It may be in a desert, days of travel away from the settled lands, yet it traverses that distance despite its length and its blindness, until it unerringly comes upon a fennel plant in some gardens, rubs its eyes with it, and returns seeing, by the permission of Allah. And Allah's guidance of man toward what is countless of his benefits and innumerable of his needs, in his foods and his medicines, and in the matters of his worldly life and his religion, and the inspirations given to beasts, birds and creeping things of the earth:

is a vast domain and a remote course (shawt batin), which no describer can encompass with description. So glory be to my Lord, the Most High.

It is also read: "qadar" (with the letter dal lightened).

"Ahwa" (dark-green) is an attribute of "ghutha'" (debris, dry refuse): that is, He brought forth the pasture (al-mar'a), made it grow, then after its greenness and freshness turned it into "ghutha' ahwa" (debris, dark-hued), i.e., dried-up (darbana) black. It is also permissible for "ahwa" to be a circumstantial adjective (hal) of "al-mar'a," meaning: He brought it forth dark and black from the intensity of its greenness and moisture, then made it debris after its dark greenness.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 87, verse 6–7:

God gave him (the Prophet) a clear sign, namely that Jibril would recite to him what was revealed, while he was unlettered (ummi), unable to write or read, and he would memorize it and not forget it, "except what God wills" (illa ma sha'a Allah), so He would make it go from his memory by abrogating its ruling and its recitation, like His saying: ﴿or We cause it to be forgotten﴾ [2:106]. It was also said: he used to hasten with the recitation when Jibril prompted him, so it was said to him: "Do not hasten, for Jibril is commanded to recite it to you repeatedly until you memorize it, and then you will not forget it except what God wills, and then you will recall it after forgetting." Or it was said: "except what God wills" means little and rare, as it is narrated that he dropped a verse in his recitation during prayer, so Ubayy thought it had been abrogated, and he asked him, and he said: "I forgot it." [Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Nasa'i, and al-Bukhari in Juz' al-Qira'ah, and al-Tabari from the narration of Zirr from Sa'id ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza from his father, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ prayed the dawn prayer and recited a verse, and he mentioned the hadith. Abu Bishr al-Dulabi also narrated it through this route, saying: from Sa'id from his father from Ubayy ibn Ka'b ... and he mentioned it.] Or it was said: "except what God wills" is meant to negate forgetting altogether, as a man says to his companion, "You are my partner in what I own, except what God wills," not intending to exclude anything; this is the use of paucity in the sense of negation. It was also said: His saying ﴿fa-la tansa﴾ is in the prohibitive form, and the alif is added for the closing rhyme, like His saying ﴿al-sabila﴾; meaning: do not neglect its recitation and repetition so that you forget it, except what God wills to make you forget by lifting its recitation for the sake of a benefit. ﴿Indeed He knows the open (al-jahr)﴾, meaning that you raise your voice in recitation along with Jibril's recitation out of fear of lapse, and God knows your raising of your voice with him and what is in your soul that prompts you to raise it; so do not do so, for I will suffice you in what you fear. Or He knows what you conceal and what you declare of your words and deeds, and what is apparent and hidden of your conditions, and what is a benefit to you in your religion and a corruption in it, so He causes to be forgotten from the revelation what He wills, and keeps memorized what He wills.

﴿وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرى﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with ﴿سَنُقْرِئُكَ﴾ (ma'tuf, a coordinating conjunction linking it to the preceding clause). The statement ﴿إِنَّهُ يَعْلَمُ الْجَهْرَ وَما يَخْفى﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh, a clause placed between related parts of a sentence without changing their grammatical connection). Its meaning: ﴿We will facilitate for you the way that is easier and simpler﴾, that is, preserving the revelation [[Al-Zamakhshari's phrase "يعنى حفظ الوحي" is probably meant as "يعنى في حفظ الوحي" (i.e., in preserving the revelation). (ʿ)]]. It was also said that it refers to the tolerant Sharia (al-shari'a al-samha, the lenient religious law), which is the easiest of the laws and the simplest in its sources. It was also said: We will make you successful in doing the deeds of Paradise.

If you ask: The Messenger ﷺ was commanded to remind, whether the reminder benefited or not, so what is the meaning of making benefit a condition?

I say: It has two aspects. The first: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had exhausted his effort in admonishing them, and they only increased in rebellion and transgression with every increase in reminder. The Prophet ﷺ was consumed by grief and anguish, and he grew more eager and zealous in admonishing them. So it was said to him: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller. So remind, by the Qur'an, whoever fears My warning﴾, or ﴿turn away from them and say, "Peace"﴾. Thus, ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾, and this is after establishing the proof by repeating the admonition. The second: that its apparent form is a condition, but its meaning is a rebuke of those who admonish, an information about their state, a denial of the reminder's effect on them, and a recording against them of being sealed upon their hearts. Like when you say to a preacher: "Admonish the tax-collectors, if they listen to you," intending by this condition to deny that, and that it will not happen. ﴿Whoever fears Allah and the evil consequence will be reminded﴾, so he will consider and reflect until consideration leads him to follow the truth.

As for these people, they neither fear nor reflect, so do not hope that they will accept from you.

﴿and the wretched one will avoid it﴾, that is, avoids the reminder and shuns it. ﴿The wretched﴾ refers to the disbeliever, because he is more wretched than the wrongdoer, or it means the one who is the most wretched of the disbelievers, because of his extreme enmity toward the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It was said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa.

﴿the greatest Fire﴾: the lowest of the layers of Hell. [[Mahmud said: "al-Ashqa: the disbeliever, because he is more wretched than the wrongdoer. And al-Nar al-Kubra: the lowest of the layers of the Fire." Ahmad says: he points to the eternal abiding of the wrongdoer together with the disbeliever in the lowest parts of the Fire, while the wrongdoer is higher than him, as he explicitly stated many times before.]] It was also said: al-Kubra is the Fire of Hell, and al-Sughra is the fire of this world.

It was also said: "Thumma" (then) is used because being suspended between life and death is more dreadful than burning, so it is delayed relative to it in degrees of severity. The meaning: he neither dies and finds rest, nor lives a life that benefits him.

This is a reference to His words, "He has succeeded who purifies himself" up to "and what remains," meaning that the sense of this statement is found in those scrolls. It was also said: it refers to what is in the whole surah.

It is related from Abu Dhar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How many books has Allah sent down?" He said: "One hundred and four books. Of them, upon Adam: ten scrolls; upon Shith: fifty scrolls; upon Akhnukh, who is Idris: thirty scrolls; upon Ibrahim: ten scrolls; and the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Furqan."
